1.patient_information_and_chief_complain.text: A 25-year-old male patient presented with the chief complaint of "cough for 1 month, fever for 10 days, and shortness of breath for 7 days." One month earlier, the patient developed a cough with a small amount of white sputum without an obvious precipitating cause. Chest CT at an outside hospital suggested "pneumonia." He received IV levofloxacin for 2 days, and the cough was slightly relieved, but recurred after discontinuation. Ten days earlier, the patient developed fever with a temperature of around 38℃. Seven days earlier, he developed shortness of breath with progressive worsening. Chest CT at an outside hospital suggested "bilateral bronchiectasis with infection and left pleural effusion," and arterial blood gas analysis indicated type I respiratory failure. He was treated with IV cefoperazone sodium/sulbactam sodium and thoracentesis with pleural fluid drainage, but symptoms did not improve. Two days earlier, the patient's shortness of breath worsened during IV infusion at the outside hospital, and he was urgently admitted to our hospital. Chest CT showed "bilateral interlobular septal thickening, bilateral patchy infiltrative opacities, and fluid in the pericardium, bilateral pleural cavities, and interlobar fissures." A left closed thoracic drainage procedure was performed. Pleural fluid biochemistry and routine testing showed exudative fluid. Past medical history: bronchial asthma for 5 years. Personal history: occasional smoking and alcohol use. Unmarried, no children. Family history: unremarkable. Physical examination: T 38.8℃, P 135 beats/min, R 28 breaths/min, BP 132/80mmHg. Alert, anxious, transported into the ward by stretcher. No enlargement of superficial lymph nodes was palpable throughout the body. Cyanosis of the lips. Neck supple, no resistance. Left chest drainage tube in place. Dullness to percussion over the left lower lung, decreased breath sounds in the left lower lung, and diffuse wheezing audible in both lungs. Cardiac dullness slightly enlarged, heart rate 135 beats/min, regular rhythm, distant heart sounds, no pathologic murmur heard in any valve auscultation area, and no pericardial friction rub. No obvious abnormalities were found on abdominal, spinal, or neurologic examination. Ancillary studies: Chest CT (Day 0, our hospital): bilateral interlobular septal thickening; increased bilateral lung markings, thickening of the bronchial walls bilaterally, scattered patchy infiltrative opacities in both lungs distributed along the bronchovascular bundles; bilateral pleural effusions and pericardial effusion. Arterial blood gas analysis (Day +2, our hospital): pH 7.468, PaCO2 34.4mmHg, PaO2 47.3mmHg, type I respiratory failure. Preliminary diagnosis: bilateral pulmonary lesions of undetermined nature.

differential_diagnoses.name: Severe community-acquired pneumonia (atypical pathogen or mixed infection) with pleural effusion and pericardial effusion
supporting_evidence: Cough for 1 month, fever for 10 days, and shortness of breath for 7 days with progressive worsening, consistent with manifestations of an infectious pulmonary disease
Temperature 38.8℃, respiratory rate 28 breaths/min, heart rate 135 beats/min, suggesting an acute severe course

Chest CT showed scattered patchy infiltrative opacities in both lungs distributed along the bronchovascular bundles, increased bilateral lung markings, and thickening of the bronchial walls bilaterally

CT at both the outside hospital and our hospital showed bilateral pleural effusions, and pleural fluid biochemistry and routine testing indicated exudative fluid, supporting inflammatory serosal cavity involvement.
Arterial blood gas analysis showed PaO2 47.3 mmHg, consistent with type I respiratory failure, indicating that the pulmonary lesion has caused severe oxygenation impairment.
Phase I correlated images show multiple patchy/linear areas of consolidation or exudative opacities in both lungs, accompanied by bilateral pleural effusions
opposing_evidence: After sequential treatment with levofloxacin, cefoperazone sodium/sulbactam sodium, and pleural drainage, symptoms did not improve significantly, suggesting that common bacterial pneumonia cannot fully explain the condition.
The concomitant presence of pericardial effusion and distant heart sounds is more suggestive of a systemic process or polyserosal cavity involvement than simple pneumonia.

differential_diagnoses.name: Tuberculosis (pulmonary tuberculosis complicated by tuberculous pleuritis/pericarditis)
supporting_evidence: Young man, cough for 1 month, progressively worsening fever and shortness of breath, subacute course
The pleural effusion is exudative, and bilateral pleural effusions and pericardial effusion are present, suggesting possible tuberculous involvement of multiple serous cavities.
No improvement in symptoms after conventional antibacterial therapy, supporting the possibility of a non-common bacterial infection

Chest CT showed scattered patchy infiltrative opacities in both lungs, distributed along the bronchovascular bundles, with interlobular septal thickening, which may be seen in some tuberculosis-related pulmonary involvement patterns.
Phase I correlated images show bilateral pleural effusions and a relatively enlarged cardiac silhouette/pericardial effusion findings.
opposing_evidence: The first-stage information did not mention clues such as night sweats, weight loss, a definite history of TB exposure, or typical upper lobe cavitation.
No enlargement of superficial lymph nodes was palpable throughout the body; no other evidence of TB was provided

differential_diagnoses.name: Pulmonary infiltration with pleural and pericardial effusions caused by lymphoma or other hematologic malignancies
supporting_evidence: A 25-year-old young patient with bilateral lung lesions complicated by bilateral pleural effusions and pericardial effusion, suggesting that in addition to infection, neoplastic or hematologic disease should also be considered.

Chest CT showed interlobular septal thickening in both lungs and patchy infiltrative opacities distributed along the bronchovascular bundles; this perilymphatic distribution can be seen in tumor-related infiltration.
No improvement with routine anti-infective treatment, supporting the possibility of a non-common infectious lesion
The cardiac dullness border is slightly enlarged, heart sounds are distant, and there is pericardial effusion, suggesting a possible systemic process with mediastinal/serosal involvement.
Phase 1 associated images show bilateral pleural effusions and pericardial effusion.
opposing_evidence: No enlargement of superficial lymph nodes was palpable throughout the body
The information from the first stage did not provide more direct evidence supporting a hematologic malignancy, such as weight loss, night sweats, hepatosplenomegaly, or a prominent mediastinal mass.

differential_diagnoses.name: Diffuse alveolar hemorrhage/ANCA-associated vasculitis and other systemic immune-mediated diseases involving the lungs and serous cavities
supporting_evidence: Diffuse patchy infiltrative opacities in both lungs, interlobular septal thickening, and rapidly developing severe hypoxemia warrant vigilance for noninfectious diffuse lung injury
The concomitant presence of pleural effusion and pericardial effusion suggests possible multiorgan involvement of a systemic inflammatory disease.
No improvement with standard anti-infective treatment, supporting a cause other than infection
Stage 1 correlated images show bilateral pulmonary lesions with bilateral pleural effusion
opposing_evidence: The Phase 1 information did not mention common clues to vasculitis/immune-mediated disease such as hemoptysis, anemia, renal involvement, rash, sinus symptoms, or arthralgia.
Fever and productive cough can still more commonly be explained by infection

differential_diagnoses.name: Asthma-related pulmonary diseases such as eosinophilic pneumonia or allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis
supporting_evidence: History of bronchial asthma for 5 years; on physical examination, diffuse wheezing was audible in both lungs, indicating a clear background of airway hyperresponsiveness.
Cough, shortness of breath, and bilateral pulmonary infiltrates may be seen in eosinophilic pneumonia or asthma-related diseases such as ABPA.
Poor response to conventional antibacterial therapy suggests possible non-common bacterial infection
In the first stage, the associated images show lesions in both lungs distributed along the bronchovascular bundles, with bronchial wall thickening.
opposing_evidence: Pleural effusion, especially when accompanied by pericardial effusion, is not a typical manifestation of asthma-related pulmonary disease.
Stage 1 information did not provide supporting evidence such as elevated peripheral eosinophils, mucus plugging, central bronchiectasis, or a history of fungal allergy.

recommended_exams.exam: Fungal G test and GM test
TB-related tests (TB antibody, TB-DNA, T-SPOT, PPD test, rapid testing of pleural and pericardial effusion for Mycobacterium tuberculosis and rifampin resistance)
Multiple blood cultures, pleural effusion bacterial culture, and pericardial effusion bacterial culture
Repeated exfoliative cytology examinations of pleural effusion and pericardial effusion, paraffin blocks, and DNA aneuploid cells

stage2_input.text: Routine laboratory tests: CBC: WBC 12.4×10^9/L, EOS% 53.71%, EOS 6.66×10^9/L; stool routine: occult blood positive; coagulation panel: D-dimer 5200 ug/L, FDP 17.9 mg/L; cardiac enzymes: LDH 325 U/L; BNP: 109 pg/ml; troponin I: 0.48 ng/ml; urinalysis, liver and kidney function, electrolytes, hepatitis panel + HIV + TP showed no abnormalities. Inflammatory markers: ESR: 50 mm/h; HsCRP: 160 mg/L; cytokine panel: hIL-2R 2967 U/ml, IL-6 55.7 pg/ml, IL-8 120 pg/ml. Infectious disease markers: endotoxin and PCT normal; atypical pathogens: Mycoplasma antibody IgM, Chlamydia antibody IgM, and Legionella pneumophila antibody IgM all negative; fungi: G test and GM test negative; viruses: adenovirus antibody IgM, respiratory syncytial virus antibody IgM, influenza A virus antibody IgM, influenza B virus antibody IgM, and parainfluenza virus antibody IgM all negative; tuberculosis: TB antibody, TB-DNA, T-spot, and PPD test all negative; rapid testing for Mycobacterium tuberculosis and rifampin resistance in pleural and pericardial effusion, TB antibody, and TB-DNA all negative; cultures: multiple blood cultures, pleural fluid bacterial culture, and pericardial fluid bacterial culture were all negative. Autoimmune disease markers: autoantibodies and ANCA negative; rheumatologic panel: RF 28.5 IU/L; humoral immunity: IgE 4050 IU/L. Tumor-related markers: tumor markers: NSE 23.52 ng/ml, CA125 205.9 U/ml; repeated exfoliative cytology of pleural and pericardial effusions, paraffin block examination, and DNA ploidy abnormal cell analysis found no evidence of tumor. Others: thyroid function panel: TSH 7.9 uIU/ml, T3 1.2 nmol/L, T4 113.1 nmol/L; blood allergens: house dust mite allergy, measured value 0.67 IU/ml. Pericardial effusion and pleural effusion were exudative, with an increased eosinophil percentage.

exclusion_reasons: This patient has no evidence of fungal, parasitic, or other infection; no history of suspicious drug exposure; concomitant pulmonary opacities; and no definite evidence of tumor.

differential_diagnoses.name: Acute eosinophilic pneumonia
exclusion_reasons: Peripheral blood eosinophils are normal (elevated in the patient); if the therapeutic effect is poor, the medical history should be taken carefully.

differential_diagnoses.name: Chronic eosinophilic pneumonia
evidence: Subacute course, disease duration of several weeks or months, cough and dyspnea

differential_diagnoses.name: organizing pneumonia
exclusion_reasons: Imaging findings are nonspecific, most often bilateral patchy infiltrates; migratory changes are often seen during the course of the disease.

differential_diagnoses.name: Langerhans cell histiocytosis
exclusion_reasons: Early imaging manifestations are irregular nodular opacities 1-10 mm in diameter, symmetrically distributed in the bilateral upper and middle lung fields; these gradually evolve into cavitary nodules, thick-walled cavities, and thin-walled cavities. In the intermediate stage, they progress to cystic opacities, and in the late stage, honeycomb change appears. Pneumothorax is common, and pleural effusion is uncommon.

differential_diagnoses.name: Hypereosinophilic syndrome (HES)
evidence: The patient has marked eosinophilia; hypereosinophilia, tissue hypereosinophilia, and hypereosinophilic syndrome should be considered.
exclusion_reasons: Other diseases must be excluded before a diagnosis of HES can be made

recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: Bone marrow aspiration result: markedly active bone marrow hyperplasia, normal megakaryocyte count, markedly increased reticulocyte proportion, eosinophils readily seen in the bone marrow (7%), increased total peripheral white blood cell count, predominantly mature granulocytes, with no evidence of hematologic malignancy.
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: The patient is a young man with a history of asthma. He presented this time with cough, fever, progressive dyspnea, bilateral pulmonary infiltrates, pleural effusion, and pericardial effusion, and was subsequently found to have marked peripheral blood eosinophilia, suggesting that eosinophilia-related disorders should be strongly considered in addition to infection. The purpose of bone marrow aspiration is first to determine whether the eosinophilia originates from a primary/clonal bone marrow abnormality and to exclude hematologic malignancies such as leukemia and myeloproliferative disorders; second, in conjunction with increased bone marrow eosinophils but no evidence of malignancy, this result supports secondary or immune-related eosinophilia and is more helpful in focusing the diagnostic direction on EGPA/HES. This examination is directly related to the diagnostic pathway and treatment selection, because if a hematologic malignancy is present, the treatment strategy is completely different from glucocorticoid/immunosuppressive regimens.

recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: Complete blood count (Day -29): WBC 10.6×10^9/L, E% 30.47%, E 3.23×10^9/L.
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: During the course of the illness, the patient developed fever, hypoxemic respiratory failure, and bilateral lung lesions, with a poor response to conventional anti-infective therapy; the complete blood count is one of the most fundamental and most critical dynamic tests. In this patient, the complete blood count indicated marked eosinophilia, which, together with the history of asthma, pulmonary infiltrates, pleural and pericardial effusions, and subsequent neurologic involvement, constitutes important evidence supporting a shift from infectious pneumonia to an eosinophil-associated systemic disease. Repeated monitoring of the complete blood count can confirm the persistence and severity of eosinophilia, help assess disease activity and the response to glucocorticoid and immunosuppressive therapy, and provide a basis for the differential diagnosis of EGPA, hypereosinophilic syndrome, and chronic eosinophilic pneumonia.

recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: Further sinus CT showed: pansinusitis, possible left maxillary sinus cyst, and nasal septal deviation.
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: The patient has a clear history of asthma, together with markedly elevated peripheral eosinophils, a tendency toward migratory pulmonary infiltrates, and effusions in multiple serous cavities, suggesting that eosinophilic vasculitis such as EGPA should be considered. Sinus involvement is a common component of EGPA, but symptoms alone may not be sufficient; sinus CT can objectively identify evidence of upper airway involvement. The examination showed pansinusitis, which, together with asthma and eosinophilia, constitutes an important clue for the classification and diagnosis of EGPA, helps explain the background of systemic allergic/eosinophilic inflammation, and helps exclude clinical manifestations that cannot be fully explained by simple infectious pneumonia alone. The significance of this examination is that it supplements the sinusitis evidence in the diagnostic criteria, increases diagnostic confidence for EGPA, and supports subsequent treatment decisions regarding glucocorticoids and immunosuppressive therapy.

recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: Electromyography: complete injury of the left lower extremity sural nerve; moderate injury of the tibial nerve, predominantly axonal changes.
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: After hospitalization, the patient developed left foot pain, numbness of the left lower leg, and difficulty walking, suggesting possible peripheral nerve involvement. In patients with asthma, marked eosinophilia, and pulmonary infiltrates, mononeuropathy or polyneuropathy is an extremely important manifestation of systemic involvement in EGPA. Electromyography can objectively determine whether nerve injury is present, the distribution of the affected nerves, and the nature of the injury, and distinguish vasculitic axonal injury from weakness or sensory abnormalities caused by other reasons. The examination results confirmed peripheral neuropathy of the left lower extremity, resolving the key clinical question of whether there was multi-organ involvement, significantly increasing the diagnostic confidence for EGPA, and indicating that the disease had extended beyond isolated pulmonary disease, directly affecting whether subsequent treatment would require steroid pulse therapy and more aggressive systemic therapy combined with cyclophosphamide.

recommended_exams.exam: Bilateral lower extremity deep vein examination
recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: Bilateral lower-extremity deep vein evaluation showed no definite thrombosis
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: The patient had progressive dyspnea, severe hypoxemia, markedly elevated D-dimer, and was ultimately confirmed to have pulmonary embolism; therefore, it was necessary to identify the source of thrombosis and assess the venous thromboembolism burden. Bilateral lower-extremity deep vein evaluation is the most direct, low-risk method for screening for lower-extremity deep vein thrombosis. Although no definite thrombus was identified in this case, this negative result still has clinical value: on the one hand, it helps assess whether the pulmonary embolism originated from the lower-extremity veins; on the other hand, it suggests that under EGPA or a hypereosinophilic state, there may be in situ thrombosis or an embolic source at another site, rather than embolization from a typical DVT. This examination helps refine the etiologic assessment of pulmonary embolism, evaluate the risk of recurrence, and provide a basis for formulating an anticoagulation treatment plan.

recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: CTPA: filling defect in the pulmonary artery of the anteromedial basal segment of the left lower lobe, consider pulmonary embolism.
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: The patient was admitted with progressively worsening dyspnea and type I respiratory failure. Although chest CT showed bilateral pulmonary infiltrates, pleural effusion, and pericardial effusion, routine anti-infective treatment was ineffective, and the D-dimer was markedly elevated, indicating that pneumonia alone could not explain all of the hypoxemia and dyspnea, and pulmonary thromboembolism had to be ruled out. CTPA is the key imaging study for confirming intraluminal filling defects in the pulmonary arteries and directly addresses the urgent clinical question of whether pulmonary embolism is present. The result not only explained part of the source of the patient's severe hypoxemia and dyspnea, but also suggested that the eosinophilic inflammation/vasculitic state might be accompanied by hypercoagulability and thrombosis. This examination played a निर्णायक role in confirming the complication, assessing disease severity, and promptly initiating anticoagulant therapy.

recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: Echocardiography: intracardiac structures are roughly normal, left ventricular function measurements are within the normal range, status post pericardial effusion drainage.
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: At admission, the patient had marked tachycardia and distant heart sounds; chest CT showed pericardial effusion, and troponin and BNP were also abnormal, suggesting that in addition to pulmonary lesions, cardiac/pericardial involvement should be considered. Bedside echocardiography can dynamically assess the volume of pericardial effusion, whether there are signs of cardiac tamponade, and right and left heart function and structural abnormalities, thereby determining whether dyspnea and hypoxemia are accompanied by a cardiogenic component. In patients with eosinophilia and suspected EGPA, cardiac involvement can significantly affect prognosis and treatment intensity; therefore, this examination is used both to assess examination risk and disease severity and to help exclude major cardiac dysfunction. The results showed that the intracardiac structures and left heart function were generally normal and were consistent with status post pericardial effusion drainage, supporting that the current dyspnea was not primarily caused by left heart failure and providing a basis for subsequent treatment mainly with glucocorticoids, immunosuppression, and anticoagulation.

7.key_confirmatory_exam_information.text: Bone marrow aspiration result: markedly active bone marrow hyperplasia, normal number of megakaryocytes, markedly increased reticulocyte proportion, eosinophils readily seen in the bone marrow (7%), increased total peripheral white blood cell count, predominantly mature granulocytes, with no evidence of hematologic malignancy. CBC (Day -29): WBC 10.6×10^9/L, E% 30.47%, E 3.23×10^9/L. Further sinus CT showed: pansinusitis, possible left maxillary sinus cyst, and deviated nasal septum. Electromyography: complete injury of the left lower extremity sural nerve, moderate injury of the tibial nerve, predominantly axonal changes. Bilateral lower extremity deep vein examination showed no definite thrombus; CTPA: filling defect in the pulmonary artery of the anteromedial basal segment of the left lower lobe, consider pulmonary embolism. Echocardiography: intracardiac structures generally normal, left heart function measurements within the normal range, status post pericardial effusion drainage.

8.final_diagnosis_and_diagnostic_basis.final_diagnosis: Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis; type I respiratory failure; pleural effusion (bilateral); pericardial effusion; pulmonary embolism; hypoproteinemia.
diagnostic_basis: Meets 4 of the diagnostic criteria for eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (EGPA) (asthma-like symptoms, eosinophilia, mononeuropathy or polyneuropathy, nonfixed pulmonary infiltrates, sinusitis, etc.)
CTPA: filling defect in the pulmonary artery of the anteromedial basal segment of the left lower lobe, suspicious for pulmonary embolism

treatment_plan: Montelukast sodium, 1 tablet, once nightly, orally
Methylprednisolone 500 mg qd IV infusion for 3 days, combined with cyclophosphamide 400 mg IV infusion once weekly regimen
After pulse corticosteroid therapy, prednisone acetate was increased to 50 mg/day orally
Mycophenolate mofetil 0.5 g orally twice daily
Cyclophosphamide 400 mg by IV drip; prednisone reduced to 35 mg/day orally
treatment_response: Repeat chest CT (Day +11): The extent of opacities in both lungs was reduced compared with before; the left pleural effusion and pericardial effusion were decreased compared with before. Respiratory failure corrected.
The patient was discharged on Day +17.

One week after discharge, the patient developed left foot pain, numbness in the left lower leg, and difficulty walking. After high-dose corticosteroid pulse therapy, the pain and numbness in the left lower extremity were markedly reduced.

On Day +38, when repeat IV infusion of cyclophosphamide was planned, urinalysis showed: red blood cell count 488.6/μl, occult blood 3+; repeat urinalysis [ED]: red blood cell count 1580.4/μl, occult blood 3+. Cyclophosphamide-induced hemorrhagic cystitis as an adverse reaction could not be completely excluded; cyclophosphamide was temporarily discontinued and replaced with mycophenolate mofetil. Multiple repeat tests continued to indicate positive urine occult blood.
Urine sediment analysis performed on Day +61 showed: red blood cells covering the entire field; dysmorphic red blood cells 60%. Glomerular hematuria cannot be excluded.
Repeat CT on Day +94 showed only chronic inflammation in the right middle lobe and the lingular segment of the left lung; echocardiography showed no abnormalities.
Follow-up through Day +283, showed stable disease.
